messages.content: I want to develop a learned plasma fluid closure that recovers collisionless plasma echoes while preserving energy under unseen forcing histories. How should I understand the two concrete requirements?

The echo requirement is predictive: on held-out forcing histories, the closure should predict echo amplitudes within 10% of the corresponding Vlasov–Poisson reference values. The energy requirement is a separate quantitative check: in an unforced case, total energy drift should remain below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods. Together, they call for a closure that captures the echo response without losing the stated energy behavior.
What is the role of the Vlasov–Poisson values here?

They are the reference values for the echo-amplitude comparison. The requirement is not merely that an echo appears, or that its amplitude looks plausible; the predicted amplitude needs to be within 10% of the corresponding Vlasov–Poisson value on held-out forcing histories.
Does “held-out forcing histories” mean the same histories used to develop the learned closure?

No. “Held-out” indicates forcing histories not used for learning the closure. That condition makes the echo-amplitude target about performance on unseen histories, rather than agreement only on histories the closure has already encountered.
And when I say collisionless plasma echoes, what part of the objective does that identify?

It identifies the behavior the fluid closure must recover. The numerical criterion focuses that goal on echo amplitudes: those amplitudes must agree with Vlasov–Poisson reference values to within 10% on the held-out forcing histories. The node does not specify a particular closure form or how that behavior must be represented internally.
Is the energy condition another comparison to Vlasov–Poisson echo amplitudes?

No. The stated energy condition concerns unforced total energy drift. It sets a limit of below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods; the Vlasov–Poisson comparison applies to echo amplitudes on held-out forcing histories.
Why keep the unforced qualifier explicit?

Because it defines where the numerical energy-drift threshold applies. “Below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods” is specified for an unforced case. The broader goal also calls for preserving energy under unseen forcing histories, but it does not give a separate numerical drift threshold for a forced case. Nor should energy preservation be read as requiring total energy to stay constant while an external forcing acts.
So the two requirements should not be collapsed into one score?

Right. One requirement bounds echo-amplitude error relative to Vlasov–Poisson reference values on held-out forcing histories. The other bounds unforced total energy drift over a stated duration. Meeting one, by itself, does not establish that the other has been met.
Does the 100 plasma periods figure say anything about how frequently energy must be measured?

No measurement frequency is specified. It states the duration over which unforced total energy drift must stay below 0.1%. It does not, on its own, prescribe sampling intervals or a particular calculation of drift.
Likewise, does “within 10%” prescribe an error formula for every possible reference amplitude?

It establishes the tolerance relative to the Vlasov–Poisson echo-amplitude reference, but the wording does not spell out a detailed error convention or special handling of reference amplitudes near zero. Those details should not be treated as already specified.
Can you put the full objective in one careful sentence?

Develop a learned plasma fluid closure that recovers collisionless plasma echoes while preserving energy under unseen forcing histories, predicts echo amplitudes within 10% of Vlasov–Poisson reference values on held-out forcing histories, and keeps unforced total energy drift below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods.

For the learned plasma fluid closure, I propose using 64 Hermite memory modes, skew-symmetric moment coupling, and discrete-gradient time stepping to recover echoes while conserving unforced energy. How do those pieces fit together?

They give the proposal three distinct parts. The 64 Hermite memory modes are intended to give the closure a way to retain information relevant to the later echo response. Skew-symmetric moment coupling is intended to structure exchanges among moments without introducing spurious energy through that coupling. Discrete-gradient time stepping is intended to preserve the unforced energy at the time-discretization level. Those are design intentions, not yet evidence that the closure meets either numerical target.
What does “memory” mean here? Is the proposal that the fluid variables alone do not have to carry all the history?

Yes, at a conceptual level. The proposed 64 Hermite memory modes provide additional state that can carry information about earlier dynamics into a later prediction. That is pertinent to collisionless plasma echoes, where the response of interest depends on how information persists before an echo appears. The proposal specifies the number and type of modes, but not a demonstrated amount of echo information they retain.
Should I describe 64 as a tested minimum or an optimal mode count?
No. Here, 64 is the proposed number of Hermite memory modes. Nothing in the proposal establishes that it is minimal, optimal, or sufficient to meet the echo-amplitude target.
How does skew-symmetric moment coupling relate to energy?

Skew-symmetry is a structural way to make a coupling represent exchanges rather than a net source of a suitably defined quadratic energy. The qualification matters: whether that intuition yields the desired energy behavior depends on the full system and its energy definition. The proposal calls for skew-symmetric moment coupling; it does not, by itself, prove energy conservation for the complete closure.
Then why include discrete-gradient time stepping as well?

Because a favorable continuous-time coupling structure and the behavior of a discrete-time update are different questions. Discrete-gradient time stepping is proposed to support conservation of unforced energy through the time update, rather than relying solely on the coupling structure. Its intended role is complementary to skew-symmetric moment coupling, not a substitute for recovering echoes.
Is it fair to say this construction conserves energy under any forcing history?

That would go beyond the proposal. Its explicit conservation aim is for unforced energy. With forcing present, energy can change because of the forcing; the broader goal is to preserve appropriate energy behavior under unseen forcing histories, not to assert that forced total energy is constant.
How does this proposal connect to the quantitative requirements we discussed?

It is meant to address both requirements, but it does not establish either one. The echo test remains prediction of echo amplitudes within 10% of Vlasov–Poisson reference values on held-out forcing histories. The energy test remains unforced total energy drift below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods. The proposed memory modes relate chiefly to capturing the echo response; the coupling and time stepping relate chiefly to the unforced energy behavior.
Could I infer the 10% echo result just from including Hermite memory modes?

No. Their inclusion offers a proposed way to retain information relevant to echoes, but the 10% requirement is an outcome measured against Vlasov–Poisson reference values on held-out forcing histories. The proposal does not report that outcome.
And does calling the time stepper a discrete-gradient method automatically establish drift below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods?

No. That name identifies the proposed approach to energy-preserving time stepping. Whether the complete unforced closure keeps total energy drift below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods is still the stated requirement, not a result supplied by the proposal.
So the careful description is a candidate architecture, with distinct roles for memory, coupling, and stepping?

Exactly. It is a proposed learned plasma fluid closure using 64 Hermite memory modes to support echo recovery, skew-symmetric moment coupling to structure energy-neutral exchanges, and discrete-gradient time stepping to target unforced energy conservation. Its performance on unseen forcing histories and its quantitative energy drift remain to be established.
Can 64 Hermite modes retain phase-mixed information across unseen forcing delays without compromising discrete-gradient energy conservation?

That is the key open question for this proposal. The 64 Hermite modes are intended to retain information that can contribute to a later echo, including when the forcing delay is unseen. Discrete-gradient time stepping is intended to conserve unforced energy. Neither intention establishes that both properties will hold together in the complete closure.
What exactly needs to persist across a forcing delay?

Information carried in the phase-mixed state that remains relevant to the later echo. The question is whether the finite set of 64 Hermite memory modes can represent enough of that information over delays the closure has not encountered during learning. It is not merely whether the modes remain numerically present; they must retain what matters for the echo response.
Does an unseen delay pose a different issue from an unseen forcing history?

It makes the question more specific. An unseen forcing delay asks whether the memory remains useful when the timing differs from what was encountered during learning. That is one aspect of generalizing to unseen forcing histories, but the question here does not claim that performance across every kind of unseen history follows from performance across delays.
Could the energy-conserving stepper itself tell us whether the memory is sufficient?

No. Conservation of an unforced energy quantity and retention of phase-mixed information are distinct properties. A time update could conserve energy yet fail to retain the information needed to predict an echo accurately. Conversely, a representation could retain useful memory without the complete numerical update satisfying the desired energy behavior.
Then what does “without compromising discrete-gradient energy conservation” ask?

It asks whether the memory modes can be incorporated into the closure while preserving the intended unforced energy-conservation property of the discrete-gradient time stepping. The relevant issue is the behavior of the complete update, including the memory modes and their coupling—not just a conservation property attributed to the stepper in isolation.
Is there a contradiction between carrying phase-mixed memory and conserving energy?

No contradiction is established by the question. Retaining information and conserving an energy quantity describe different aspects of the dynamics. But their compatibility cannot simply be assumed for this particular 64-mode closure; the way the modes participate in the full update matters.
Where does skew-symmetric moment coupling enter this question?

It is part of the proposed structure linking the moments and the memory. Its intended role is to support energy-neutral exchanges, while the Hermite modes supply memory and discrete-gradient stepping addresses the time update. The question is whether those proposed parts work together when the closure must retain phase-mixed information across unseen forcing delays.
Would exact conservation of unforced energy mean an echo amplitude must be right?

No. An energy constraint restricts one aspect of the solution, but it does not uniquely determine the echo amplitude or guarantee that the relevant phase-mixed information has been preserved. Echo recovery and energy conservation need to be considered separately, even though this question asks whether they can coexist.
Could a good echo prediction by itself establish that the discrete-gradient conservation aim survived?

No. A good echo prediction would speak to the memory and response, while the conservation question concerns unforced energy in the complete discrete update. One observation would not, by itself, establish the other property.
Should I read “64” as enough modes for every possible delay?

No. It is the specified size of the proposed Hermite memory representation. Whether 64 modes retain the needed phase-mixed information across unseen forcing delays is precisely what is being asked, not a premise already established.
And does the question assume that the discrete-gradient method fails once those modes are added?

No. It leaves the outcome open in both directions. It asks whether the 64-mode memory can support echo-relevant retention and whether doing so can leave the intended discrete-gradient energy conservation intact. It asserts neither success nor failure.
When forcing is present, should “energy conservation” mean that total energy cannot change during the delay?

Not necessarily. Forcing can change total energy. The conservation part of this question concerns the proposed discrete-gradient treatment of unforced energy; it should not be read as requiring constant total energy while forcing acts.
How can I phrase the concern without turning it into a claimed result?

You could ask: “Is a memory of 64 Hermite modes sufficient to retain the phase-mixed information needed for echoes across unseen forcing delays, while the full closure still conserves unforced energy under discrete-gradient time stepping?” That keeps both properties as questions rather than assuming either has been demonstrated.

My hypothesis is that, across held-out forcing delays, 64 Hermite modes should yield ≤10% echo-amplitude error and <0.1% unforced energy drift over 100 periods. Is that a fair way to state the prediction?

Yes, as a hypothesis rather than a reported result. It predicts two outcomes for the proposed 64-mode closure: echo-amplitude error no greater than 10% across held-out forcing delays, and unforced energy drift strictly below 0.1% over 100 periods. It does not say that either outcome has been observed.
Does “across held-out forcing delays” apply to both numbers in exactly the same way?

The echo-amplitude prediction concerns responses at held-out forcing delays. The energy-drift prediction concerns an unforced case over 100 periods. Keeping those conditions distinct avoids implying that total energy must remain constant while forcing acts.
For echo-amplitude error, what is the comparison?

In the stated goal, echo amplitudes are compared with Vlasov–Poisson reference values. Read in that context, the hypothesis predicts error of at most 10% relative to those reference amplitudes across held-out forcing delays. It does not supply measured amplitudes or a more detailed error convention.
Is “≤10%” meaningfully different from the energy bound’s “<0.1%”?
Yes. The echo-amplitude hypothesis permits an error equal to 10%; the unforced energy-drift hypothesis requires drift below 0.1%, not equal to it. Both are predicted thresholds here, not findings.
When I say 100 periods, should that be understood as the same duration as the energy requirement?

Yes. The established energy requirement specifies 100 plasma periods, and the hypothesis refers to that 100-period unforced interval. It is a duration for the energy-drift claim, not a specified forcing delay.
Does the hypothesis settle whether the 64 modes retain phase-mixed information?

No. It gives a predicted performance consequence of using 64 Hermite modes across held-out forcing delays. If the predicted echo accuracy were demonstrated, it would bear on whether the closure retains information useful for echoes, but the hypothesis itself is not a demonstration of that retention.
And does the low-drift prediction establish discrete-gradient conservation already?

No. Discrete-gradient time stepping is part of the proposed approach to conserving unforced energy. The hypothesis predicts less than 0.1% unforced energy drift over 100 periods for the closure; it does not report that the complete update has achieved that bound or prove an exact conservation property.
Would meeting only the echo-amplitude prediction count as meeting this hypothesis?
Not in full. The hypothesis joins an echo-amplitude prediction and an unforced energy-drift prediction. Evidence for one would not, by itself, establish the other.
Does this prediction cover every unseen forcing history?

It specifically names held-out forcing delays. Those are unseen timing conditions, but the wording does not establish performance for every possible unseen forcing history. The broader goal concerns unseen forcing histories; this hypothesis makes a more specific prediction about delays.
Am I claiming that 64 is the minimum number of Hermite modes needed to reach those bounds?
No. The hypothesis concerns the proposed choice of 64 Hermite modes. It neither compares mode counts nor claims that 64 is minimal or optimal.
Could I say the two thresholds would answer the earlier compatibility question if both were achieved?

They would provide evidence for the two behaviors that question puts together: accurate echoes across held-out delays and low unforced energy drift over 100 periods in the proposed closure. For now, though, the statement remains a prediction about their compatibility, not an answer established by results.

To examine the 64-mode hypothesis, I plan to generate Vlasov–Poisson two-pulse trajectories, train the 64-mode closure, then evaluate echo errors at held-out forcing delays and energy drift over 100 periods. Does that sequence match the question we are trying to answer?

Yes. The Vlasov–Poisson two-pulse trajectories provide the reference context for learning and comparing echo responses. After training the 64-mode closure, evaluating echo errors at held-out delays addresses whether it predicts echoes when the forcing timing is unseen. Evaluating unforced energy drift over 100 plasma periods addresses the separate energy requirement. This is a plan for assessing those properties, not a result.
Why specify two-pulse trajectories rather than just saying Vlasov–Poisson trajectories?

“Two-pulse” identifies the forcing setup in the plan. It matters here because the evaluation focuses on delays and the echo response associated with them. The plan does not specify pulse shapes, strengths, or a particular set of delays, so those details should remain open.
Should I say the Vlasov–Poisson trajectories are already generated?
No. Generating them is the first planned step. The wording does not report that trajectories have been produced, that the closure has been trained, or that either evaluation has taken place.
What does “held-out” require in this sequence?

The delays used to assess echo errors must be unseen during training. Otherwise the evaluation would not test the stated prediction across held-out forcing delays. The plan does not specify how many delays are held out or how they are selected.
Am I evaluating the full forcing history, or specifically the delay?

The plan specifically calls for evaluating echo errors at held-out delays in the two-pulse setting. That tests one aspect of performance on unseen forcing histories: a change in forcing timing. It does not, by itself, specify a test of every other possible variation in forcing history.
What is the echo error measured against?

The Vlasov–Poisson reference echo amplitudes. The earlier hypothesis predicts echo-amplitude error of at most 10% across held-out forcing delays. This plan says to evaluate those errors; it supplies no measured values or further error-calculation details.
Does generating trajectories and training the closure already answer whether 64 modes retain phase-mixed information?

No. Those steps prepare the closure and its reference comparison. The held-out-delay echo evaluation is the part of the plan that tests whether the trained 64-mode closure retained information useful for predicting those echoes. Even then, the plan alone does not tell us the outcome.
Where does the 100-period energy evaluation fit relative to the two-pulse tests?

It is a distinct evaluation after training. The echo errors concern the response to two-pulse forcing at held-out delays; the energy-drift requirement concerns unforced total energy over 100 plasma periods. The plan lists both evaluations without saying that energy must stay constant during the forced two-pulse trajectories.
Is it accurate to call the energy check a test of the discrete-gradient time stepping?

It can test whether the complete trained closure, which proposes discrete-gradient time stepping, exhibits the intended unforced energy behavior. The drift measurement is not automatically a proof of an exact conservation property of the stepper on its own; the full closure is what is being evaluated.
And the numerical energy target remains below 0.1% drift?

Yes. The stated requirement and hypothesis call for unforced total energy drift below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods. The plan proposes evaluating that drift; it does not say the threshold has been reached.
If the echo evaluation is good, can I skip interpreting the energy result?

No. Echo-amplitude accuracy at held-out delays and unforced energy drift are separate outcomes. The plan includes both because accurate echoes alone would not show that the proposed closure preserves unforced energy over the stated interval.
What if the energy result is good—would that establish the echo prediction?

No. Low unforced energy drift would address the energy side, not whether echo amplitudes agree with Vlasov–Poisson references at held-out delays. The two evaluations speak to different parts of the question about the 64-mode closure.
Can we describe this as a completed validation protocol?

It is a proposed sequence for evaluation, not completed validation. It specifies generating Vlasov–Poisson two-pulse trajectories, training the 64-mode closure, and evaluating held-out-delay echo errors and 100-plasma-period unforced energy drift. It does not specify every procedural detail or provide results.

Let’s run EchoDelay-v1: train the 64-mode closure on 2–8-period pulse separations, then test 9–12-period delays against Vlasov–Poisson echoes and check 100-period unforced energy drift. What does this run cover?

EchoDelay-v1 specifies a training range and two evaluations. Training uses pulse separations of 2–8 periods. Echo testing uses delays of 9–12 periods, with Vlasov–Poisson echoes as the reference. The other evaluation is unforced energy drift over 100 periods. This describes what to run; it does not report any outcomes.
Are the 9–12-period delays actually held out from the stated training range?

Yes. The 9–12-period test range lies outside the stated 2–8-period training range. In that sense, the echo test examines the closure at unseen pulse separations, rather than only at separations in the training range.
Is this testing all possible unseen forcing histories?

No. EchoDelay-v1 makes the unseen condition specific: the test delays are 9–12 periods, compared with training separations of 2–8 periods. It does not specify tests of every other possible change to a forcing history.
What does “against Vlasov–Poisson echoes” mean in the test?

It means the closure’s echo predictions at the 9–12-period delays are to be compared with Vlasov–Poisson echo references. In the context of the stated echo target, the quantity of interest is echo-amplitude error relative to those reference values. No comparison results are given here.
Should the 100-period energy-drift check be performed on the forced two-pulse response?

The specified check is unforced energy drift over 100 periods. It should be kept distinct from the forced echo comparison at the 9–12-period delays. The run description does not require total energy to remain constant while the pulses act.
So 100 periods is not another pulse separation to test?
Correct. The pulse-separation ranges are 2–8 periods for training and 9–12 periods for echo testing. The 100-period interval belongs to the unforced energy-drift evaluation.
How does EchoDelay-v1 bear on the prediction that 64 Hermite modes will handle held-out delays?

Its 9–12-period echo test is designed to examine that prediction outside the 2–8-period training range. The comparison with Vlasov–Poisson echoes can show whether the trained closure predicts the held-out-delay echo amplitudes accurately. The run specification itself does not establish whether it will.
And the energy part bears on the prediction of less than 0.1% drift?

Yes. The unforced 100-period check addresses the predicted energy behavior. The stated threshold is unforced total energy drift below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods; EchoDelay-v1 calls for checking drift over that interval, without supplying a measured value.
For the echoes, is the target still no more than 10% amplitude error?

Yes. The prediction being evaluated is echo-amplitude error of at most 10% relative to Vlasov–Poisson references on held-out delays. EchoDelay-v1 specifies the 9–12-period delays for that comparison; it does not say the target has been met.
Can we conclude that the 64-mode closure extrapolates across delays because the test range extends beyond training?

Not yet. The ranges make EchoDelay-v1 a test of performance beyond the stated training separations. Whether the closure predicts echoes accurately there depends on the test results, which have not been supplied.
Does the activity specify how many examples or which individual delays to use inside those ranges?

No. It gives the 2–8-period training range and the 9–12-period test range, but not the number of trajectories or a selection of individual separations within either range. Those details should not be assumed.
Does it specify pulse shapes or strengths?
No. EchoDelay-v1 identifies pulse separations and delays, the Vlasov–Poisson echo comparison, and the unforced energy-drift interval. It does not provide pulse shapes or strengths.
Could I call the Vlasov–Poisson echoes the training target and the test reference?

The planned work uses Vlasov–Poisson two-pulse trajectories in training and Vlasov–Poisson echoes as references for the held-out-delay test. EchoDelay-v1 does not spell out a particular training target or loss, so it is safer to state only those specified roles.
If an echo agrees with its reference, does that establish the energy-drift result?
No. The echo comparison at 9–12-period delays and the 100-period unforced energy-drift check are separate evaluations. Echo agreement would not, by itself, give the unforced drift value.
And a low unforced drift would not tell us whether echoes at 9–12 periods match Vlasov–Poisson?
Right. A low drift would address the energy side, while the echo comparison addresses predictions at held-out delays. EchoDelay-v1 includes both checks because neither substitutes for the other.
Can you restate the activity without making it sound like the results are already known?

Run EchoDelay-v1 by training the 64-mode closure on 2–8-period pulse separations, testing its echo predictions at 9–12-period delays against Vlasov–Poisson echoes, and evaluating unforced energy drift over 100 periods. The activity specifies those comparisons, not their results.
EchoDelay-v1 yielded 8.6% maximum echo-amplitude error at 9–12-period delays and 0.06% unforced energy drift after 100 periods. How should I report those results?

Report them as two measured outcomes of EchoDelay-v1: the maximum echo-amplitude error in the tested 9–12-period delay range was 8.6%, and unforced energy drift after 100 periods was 0.06%. Keep the echo comparison and the unforced energy measurement distinct, since they concern different conditions.
Does “maximum echo-amplitude error” mean 8.6% was the average across the test delays?
No. It identifies the largest reported echo-amplitude error among the evaluated 9–12-period delays. The result does not give an average error or the error at each delay.
Can I say every delay between 9 and 12 periods was tested?

Not from this result alone. It identifies the 9–12-period test range, but does not specify which individual delays were evaluated or how densely the range was sampled. The 8.6% maximum applies to the evaluations reported for EchoDelay-v1.
What were those echo amplitudes compared with?

EchoDelay-v1 compares the closure’s echoes with Vlasov–Poisson echoes at the test delays. The 8.6% figure is the reported maximum echo-amplitude error in that comparison. No individual amplitudes are provided.
Does the result identify which delay gave the maximum error?
No. It locates the maximum within the tested 9–12-period delay range, but does not identify a particular delay or provide a delay-by-delay breakdown.
The closure was trained on 2–8-period pulse separations. What can I say about the 9–12-period result in that context?

Those test delays are outside the stated 2–8-period training range, so the reported error concerns held-out pulse separations in EchoDelay-v1. The result is specific to that test range; it does not quantify performance at other unseen delays or under every unseen forcing history.
Does the 8.6% error show that the 64 Hermite modes retained all the phase-mixed information?

It reports how accurately the closure predicted echo amplitudes in this test. That is relevant to the question of retaining echo-relevant information, but it does not measure whether all phase-mixed information was retained or describe what the modes represented internally.
Is there any information here about echo timing or shape?

No separate timing or shape result is stated. The reported echo quantity is maximum amplitude error at the 9–12-period delays. It would go beyond this evidence to assign numerical accuracy to other features of the echoes.
Turning to energy, does 0.06% refer to a forced two-pulse trajectory?
No. The reported 0.06% is unforced energy drift after 100 periods. The two-pulse setup supplies the held-out-delay echo comparison; the energy figure refers to the unforced condition.
Does “after 100 periods” mean the energy drift was 0.06% at every earlier time?

No. It gives the reported drift after the 100-period interval. Without intermediate measurements, it does not describe the drift at every point during that interval or establish its largest interim value.
Can I call that exact energy conservation by the discrete-gradient update?

The evidence reports 0.06% unforced energy drift after 100 periods. It does not report zero drift or provide a proof about the complete discrete-gradient update. The measured drift is the precise claim to make here.
Does it say what happened to total energy while the two pulses were applied?
No forced-energy result is given. The reported energy measurement is unforced, so it should not be presented as a measurement of energy change during the two-pulse forcing.
Are there enough details to recompute either percentage independently?

Not from these reported figures alone. The evidence supplies the maximum echo-amplitude error, its test-delay range, and the unforced energy drift after 100 periods, but not the individual echo amplitudes, energy values, or detailed percentage calculations.
Should I infer that a different number of Hermite memory modes would do worse?
No. EchoDelay-v1 reports outcomes for the proposed 64-mode closure. It does not include a comparison with other mode counts, so it cannot establish how those alternatives would perform.
What is a concise statement that stays within the evidence?
“In EchoDelay-v1, the 64-mode closure had 8.6% maximum echo-amplitude error against Vlasov–Poisson echoes at tested 9–12-period delays, and 0.06% unforced energy drift after 100 periods.”

Given EchoDelay-v1, I want to retain the 64-mode closure for broader forcing-history validation. EchoDelay-v1 met both the echo-error and energy-drift thresholds. Is that the right scope for the decision?

Yes. The decision is to keep the 64-mode closure as the candidate for broader forcing-history validation. Its stated basis is that EchoDelay-v1 met both thresholds. That supports continuing with this closure, but it does not say that broader validation has already been completed.
What should “retain” convey here?

It means continuing to use the 64-mode closure for the next scope of validation. It is a decision to carry the candidate forward, not a claim that 64 modes are optimal or that no further questions remain.
Can I say the two requirements were met?

You can say that EchoDelay-v1 met both the echo-error and energy-drift thresholds. Keep the name of the evaluation attached to that conclusion: it does not establish that the thresholds will be met across all forcing histories.
Does broader forcing-history validation mean the held-out-delay result is being rejected?
No. The decision expressly relies on EchoDelay-v1 meeting both thresholds. Broader validation extends the scope of what remains to be assessed; it does not negate the stated EchoDelay-v1 result.
How should I distinguish the echo and energy conclusions when explaining why we are retaining the closure?

State them as separate reasons within the same decision: EchoDelay-v1 met the echo-error threshold and met the energy-drift threshold. The first concerns echo prediction in that evaluation; the second concerns unforced energy drift. Neither result should be used as a substitute for the other.
Does meeting the energy-drift threshold mean I can call the full method exactly energy-conserving?
No. The decision says the energy-drift threshold was met in EchoDelay-v1. That is a threshold conclusion, not an assertion of zero drift or a proof of exact conservation by the complete method.
And can I claim it now handles unseen forcing histories generally?
Not yet. Retaining the closure *for* broader forcing-history validation makes that broader assessment the purpose of continuing. The decision does not report its outcome.
Is this a decision to revise the 64 Hermite memory modes?
No revision is stated. The decision retains the 64-mode closure for the broader validation. It does not specify a change to its mode count or other design details.
Should the decision be phrased as a final endorsement of the closure?

A narrower phrasing is more accurate. EchoDelay-v1 met both stated thresholds, so the 64-mode closure is retained for broader forcing-history validation. That conveys a positive decision grounded in the reported evaluation without treating future validation as already settled.
Could meeting both thresholds be described as sufficient for this particular decision, without saying it settles the overall goal?

Yes. The decision explicitly gives that reason for retaining the closure. Its scope is whether to carry the 64-mode candidate into broader forcing-history validation, not whether its performance under all unseen forcing histories has been established.
Give me a concise decision statement.
Retain the 64-mode closure for broader forcing-history validation because EchoDelay-v1 met both the echo-error and energy-drift thresholds.

For the broader validation, I plan to use EchoHistory-v2’s unseen three-pulse and chirped drives with the retained 64-mode closure, measuring echo error and post-drive energy drift. What does this plan test?

It tests the retained closure on forcing histories identified as unseen, using both three-pulse and chirped drives. The two measurements address different aspects of its behavior: echo error concerns the predicted echo response, while post-drive energy drift concerns energy behavior after a drive. EchoHistory-v2 is a planned validation here; no results are stated.
Are three-pulse and chirped drives two names for the same forcing history?

The plan names them separately. It does not say whether any individual drive has both features, so it is safest to describe EchoHistory-v2 as including unseen three-pulse drives and unseen chirped drives without specifying how they overlap.
What does “unseen” qualify?

It qualifies the drive histories used for this validation. The point is to assess the retained 64-mode closure on those histories rather than presume that behavior on previously encountered forcing carries over. The plan does not specify the precise procedure used to keep the histories unseen.
Does the plan say to change the number of Hermite modes for EchoHistory-v2?
No. It calls for validating the retained 64-mode closure. It does not specify a change in mode count or a revised closure.
Does it say to retrain the closure before measuring anything?

No retraining step is stated. The wording is to validate the retained closure on EchoHistory-v2’s unseen drives. It should not be expanded into a particular training or adaptation procedure without further information.
For the echo measurement, should I assume EchoHistory-v2 has already produced reference values?

No. Measuring echo error implies a comparison, and Vlasov–Poisson echoes are the established reference for this project, but this plan does not report reference values or say that the EchoHistory-v2 measurements have been made.
Can I apply a particular numerical echo-error result to the three-pulse and chirped drives now?
No. The plan says to measure echo error on those unseen drives. It supplies no EchoHistory-v2 error values, so their echo accuracy remains an open outcome of this validation.
Does “post-drive energy drift” mean total energy must stay constant while a drive is acting?

No. “Post-drive” points to energy behavior after a drive, not a requirement that energy stay constant during forcing. The plan does not specify the energy-drift measurement interval or a numerical limit for this post-drive check.
Is that post-drive measurement identical to the earlier 100-period unforced check?

They should not be treated as identical from this wording alone. This plan specifically calls for measuring post-drive energy drift for EchoHistory-v2; it does not state a 100-period interval or define its measurement procedure. The distinction is that these cases have a preceding drive.
What can we infer about how long the post-drive observation lasts?
